lessonTitle: Upper and Lower Gastrointestinal Disease: Peptic Ulcer, Inflammatory Bowel Disease and Colorectal Cancer

blocks.text: A 45-year-old teacher has a gnawing epigastric pain that wakes him at 2 a.m. and is eased by a snack, and that has been recurring for months. At endoscopy there is a 6 mm punched-out ulcer in the first part of the duodenum. A small biopsy of the stomach shows a curved bacterium living beneath the mucus layer. A single infection, or a common painkiller, is behind most such ulcers.

blocks.markdown: The gastric mucosa is protected by a **mucus-bicarbonate barrier**, rich mucosal blood flow and prostaglandins, while gastric acid (hydrochloric acid from parietal cells) and pepsin attack it. A **peptic ulcer** is a defect in the mucosa extending through the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa or deeper, in the stomach or duodenum, and results from an imbalance in favour of aggression over defence. The two dominant causes are *Helicobacter pylori* infection and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).

### Helicobacter pylori and NSAIDs

*H. pylori* is a spiral Gram-negative bacterium that colonises the gastric mucus. It makes **urease**, which converts urea to ammonia, buffering acid in its immediate surroundings so that it survives, and it releases toxins that injure epithelium. Chronic infection causes gastritis. If the gastritis is antral-predominant, acid output is high and duodenal ulcer results; if it involves the body, acid falls and gastric ulcer or gastric cancer risk rises. It is also associated with gastric MALT lymphoma. **NSAIDs** inhibit cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), reducing synthesis of the protective prostaglandins that sustain mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow, and so permit acid injury, including from systemic effect after absorption. Diagnosis of *H. pylori* uses the urea breath test or stool antigen test (proton pump inhibitors must be stopped beforehand, as they can cause false negatives); eradication uses a proton pump inhibitor with antibiotics, and stopping NSAIDs where possible heals NSAID ulcers.

blocks.title: How much does acid suppression change gastric acidity?
blocks.prompt: Fasting gastric pH is 2.0. A proton pump inhibitor raises it to 3.0. By what factor has hydrogen ion concentration fallen?

steps.text: The ratio is 0.01 / 0.001 = 10, so acid concentration has fallen ten-fold.

blocks.answer: Hydrogen ion concentration has fallen ten-fold.

rows: Majority, though NSAIDs account for many
Often relieved by eating; may wake at night
Often worsened by eating, with weight loss
May be malignant, so biopsy and healing check

blocks.markdown:
### Inflammatory bowel disease

Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis are the two chronic idiopathic inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), arising from a dysregulated mucosal immune response to gut flora in genetically susceptible people. **Crohn disease** can affect any part of the gut from mouth to anus, most often the terminal ileum, with **skip lesions** (diseased segments between normal bowel), **transmural** inflammation, **non-caseating granulomas**, deep fissuring ulcers giving a cobblestone mucosa, and complications such as strictures, fistulae and perianal disease. **Ulcerative colitis (UC)** is limited to the colon, begins in the rectum and extends **continuously** proximally; inflammation is confined to the **mucosa and submucosa** with crypt abscesses and, in chronic disease, pseudopolyps and loss of haustra.

rows: Mouth to anus; terminal ileum commonly; skip lesions
Colon only; rectum involved, continuous spread
Crypt abscesses, goblet cell depletion; no granulomas
Abdominal pain, diarrhoea, weight loss; blood less prominent
Toxic megacolon, colorectal cancer; primary sclerosing cholangitis

blocks.markdown:
### Colorectal cancer and alarm symptoms

Most colorectal cancers arise from adenomatous polyps through the **adenoma-carcinoma sequence**, involving accumulating mutations (loss of the APC tumour suppressor early, then KRAS activation and loss of p53). Risk factors include age, family history, IBD, low fibre and high red or processed meat intake, obesity and smoking. Early cancer is often silent, so symptoms matter. **Alarm symptoms** prompting urgent investigation include persistent **rectal bleeding**, a **persistent change in bowel habit** (generally over about 6 weeks), **iron-deficiency anaemia** without obvious cause (especially in older adults and in men and postmenopausal women), **unexplained weight loss**, a palpable abdominal or rectal mass, and rectal tenesmus. The faecal immunochemical test (FIT) for occult blood is used for screening and triage.

blocks.title: Applying the Crohn versus UC discriminators
blocks.prompt: A 28-year-old woman has chronic diarrhoea and weight loss. Colonoscopy shows patches of ulceration in the terminal ileum and caecum with normal mucosa between them, and biopsy shows transmural inflammation with non-caseating granulomas. Classify the disease.

steps.text: Patchy ulceration with normal intervening mucosa describes skip lesions, which do not occur in UC.
Transmural inflammation and non-caseating granulomas are histological hallmarks of Crohn disease.
Involvement of the terminal ileum, which UC does not affect (apart from mild backwash ileitis), supports the same conclusion.

blocks.title: Know the alarm features
blocks.text: Alarm symptoms do not prove cancer, but they identify patients who should be investigated, usually by colonoscopy or CT colonography. Iron-deficiency anaemia in an older adult is a colorectal cancer sign until proven otherwise.

points: Peptic ulcers arise when acid and pepsin overwhelm mucosal defences; H. pylori (urease, gastritis) and NSAIDs (COX-1 inhibition, loss of prostaglandins) are the main causes.
Crohn disease is patchy, transmural and granulomatous and can affect the whole gut, whereas ulcerative colitis is continuous from the rectum, confined to mucosa and submucosa, with crypt abscesses.
Alarm symptoms for colorectal cancer include rectal bleeding, persistent change in bowel habit, iron-deficiency anaemia, weight loss and an abdominal mass.

questions.stem: How does Helicobacter pylori survive in the acidic environment of the stomach?

options.text: It produces urease, generating ammonia that neutralises acid around it
It secretes bicarbonate through a type IV pump
It forms spores that resist acid
It colonises only the duodenum, where acid is absent

questions.correctOptionText: It produces urease, generating ammonia that neutralises acid around it

distractorRationale.a: Correct: urease converts urea to ammonia, creating a protective alkaline microenvironment.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: no such bicarbonate pump explains survival.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: H. pylori is a non-spore-forming spiral bacterium.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: it colonises the gastric antrum and body under the mucus layer.

questions.explanation: Urease hydrolyses urea to ammonia and carbon dioxide, buffering acid immediately around the bacterium. This also underlies the urea breath test.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with osteoarthritis who takes an NSAID regularly develops a gastric ulcer. Which mechanism best explains this?

options.text: COX-1 inhibition reduces protective prostaglandins, decreasing mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow
Increased gastrin release from G cells directly
Production of urease by the drug
Direct stimulation of parietal cell histamine receptors

questions.correctOptionText: COX-1 inhibition reduces protective prostaglandins, decreasing mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow

distractorRationale.a: Correct: prostaglandins maintain mucosal defence, and NSAIDs deplete them.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: NSAIDs do not primarily act through gastrin.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: urease is a bacterial enzyme of H. pylori.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: NSAIDs do not stimulate histamine receptors.

questions.explanation: Prostaglandins stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion and maintain mucosal blood flow. By blocking COX-1, NSAIDs remove this defence, leaving the mucosa vulnerable to acid and pepsin.

questions.stem: A colonoscopy in a 30-year-old man shows continuous inflammation extending from the rectum to the splenic flexure, with crypt abscesses on biopsy and no granulomas. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Ulcerative colitis
Crohn disease
Ischaemic colitis
Coeliac disease

distractorRationale.a: Correct: continuous inflammation from the rectum with crypt abscesses and no granulomas is UC.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: Crohn disease has skip lesions and granulomas.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: ischaemic colitis follows a vascular distribution and affects older patients.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: coeliac disease affects the small intestine, not the colon.

questions.explanation: Ulcerative colitis begins in the rectum and spreads proximally without skip areas, with inflammation confined to the mucosa. Crypt abscesses are characteristic.

questions.stem: A resection specimen shows transmural inflammation, fissuring ulcers, and non-caseating granulomas in a segment of ileum separated from the next affected segment by normal bowel. Which finding best identifies the disease?

options.text: Skip lesions with transmural inflammation (Crohn disease)
Pseudopolyps with mucosal-only inflammation (ulcerative colitis)
Villous atrophy with intraepithelial lymphocytes (coeliac disease)
Dysplastic adenomatous glands (colorectal adenoma)

questions.correctOptionText: Skip lesions with transmural inflammation (Crohn disease)

distractorRationale.a: Correct: skip lesions, transmural change and granulomas define Crohn disease.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: pseudopolyps and mucosal-only inflammation indicate UC.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: villous atrophy is the feature of coeliac disease.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: adenomas are dysplastic polyps and not inflammatory.

questions.explanation: Crohn disease is characterised by discontinuous segmental involvement with transmural inflammation and granulomas. This explains complications such as fistulae and strictures.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has fatigue, and blood tests show a microcytic iron-deficiency anaemia. He has no overt bleeding and no dietary cause. Which investigation is most appropriate?

options.text: Referral for colonoscopy and upper gastrointestinal evaluation
Reassurance and oral iron only
Repeat the blood test in a year
Thyroid function tests only

questions.correctOptionText: Referral for colonoscopy and upper gastrointestinal evaluation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in an older man implies occult gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: iron alone treats the effect without finding the source.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: delaying risks missing a cancer.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: thyroid testing does not address the iron deficiency.

questions.explanation: In a man of this age, iron deficiency without a dietary cause usually reflects chronic occult gastrointestinal blood loss, and colorectal cancer is a leading concern. The source must be sought by endoscopy.

questions.stem: A proton pump inhibitor raises intragastric pH from 1.5 to 4.5. By what factor does the hydrogen ion concentration fall? Give the factor as a ratio.
questions.explanation: A pH change of 3 units corresponds to 10^3, so hydrogen ion concentration falls 1000-fold. Powerful acid suppression of this size explains the healing of peptic ulcers with proton pump inhibitors.

questions.stem: A faecal immunochemical test is evaluated in 200 patients who all have confirmed colorectal cancer. It is positive in 170. Calculate its sensitivity as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Sensitivity is TP / (TP + FN) = 170 / 200 = 0.85, or 85%. The 30 missed cancers are false negatives, which is why alarm symptoms should be investigated even when a stool test is negative.

questions.stem: Explain the roles of Helicobacter pylori and NSAIDs in the pathogenesis of peptic ulcer disease and how H. pylori infection is diagnosed.
markingGuide: Ulcers form when acid and pepsin overwhelm mucosal defences
H. pylori: urease generating ammonia, chronic gastritis, toxins; antral-predominant gastritis with high acid causes duodenal ulcer
Association with gastric ulcer, gastric cancer and MALT lymphoma
NSAIDs: COX-1 inhibition reduces prostaglandins, mucus, bicarbonate and blood flow
Diagnosis: urea breath test or stool antigen; PPI should be stopped before testing
Treatment: eradication regimen with PPI plus antibiotics; stop NSAIDs where possible
questions.explanation: Both factors weaken mucosal defence rather than simply increasing acid. H. pylori injures the mucosa and alters acid secretion, while NSAIDs remove prostaglandin protection.

questions.stem: Distinguish Crohn disease from ulcerative colitis in terms of distribution, depth of inflammation, histology and complications.
markingGuide: Crohn: mouth to anus, terminal ileum commonly, skip lesions
UC: colon only, rectum involved, continuous proximal extension
Crohn: transmural inflammation; UC: mucosa and submucosa
Crohn: non-caseating granulomas, fissuring ulcers, cobblestoning
UC: crypt abscesses, goblet cell loss, pseudopolyps
Complications: Crohn strictures, fistulae, perianal disease; UC toxic megacolon, colorectal cancer, bloody diarrhoea
questions.explanation: The differences in depth and distribution explain the clinical features: transmural disease leads to strictures and fistulae, while mucosal disease causes bleeding and diarrhoea. Histology provides the most reliable discriminator.

questions.stem: Describe the adenoma-carcinoma sequence and list the alarm symptoms that should prompt investigation for colorectal cancer, explaining why early cancer may be asymptomatic.
markingGuide: Adenomatous polyp progresses to carcinoma through accumulated mutations
Early APC loss, then KRAS activation and p53 loss
Alarm symptoms: rectal bleeding, persistent change in bowel habit, iron-deficiency anaemia, weight loss, abdominal or rectal mass, tenesmus
Early tumours are small and do not obstruct or bleed enough to be noticed
Investigation by colonoscopy or imaging; FIT for screening
questions.explanation: The long dysplastic phase before invasion offers a window for detection. Early lesions bleed minimally or not at all, so symptoms usually appear when disease is advanced, which is why alarm features lower the threshold for investigation.
